utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Madam Registrar and good morning, everyone. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are present. Mr. McCloskey alone -- is alone today representing the Prosecution. Absent amongst the Defence teams is, I see, Ms. Tapuskovic, Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Haynes. Yes. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We were at 3957, if we could go back to that and give Colonel -- good morning, Colonel. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Back to that 14 July order that went out in your name, I think you've told us you got that information from General Djukic, but you don't remember where Djukic was when he gave you this information; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, Your Honours, it's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could he have been at, you know, at Han Pijesak or would this be something that you received over the telephone or radio?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received this telephone from him via telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And if we look at the back of it, we can see that it was received by a unit at 2325 hours on the 14th, so relatively -- well, very late on the 14th. And so you would have, on the 14th, have had a chance to receive other information from what was going on in the area of Srebrenica; for example, you would have had received the logistics -- daily logistics report from the Drina Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Daily reports were coming in, but whether I did receive information about this, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you remember speaking to anyone, say, you know, Mr. Krsmanovic from the Drina Corps, Radoslav Jankovic intel from the Main Staff, Mr. Kerkez from the Main Staff, any of these people talk to you about what was going on from Potocari that day?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the name of Kuzmanovic was mentioned but I don't remember who that was. And I don't remember a single conversation about the events taking place in Srebrenica that I had with those people mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you do in paragraph 3, mention that the transportation of this filter and its accompanying equipment shall be carried out on the requisitioned transportation means trailer trucks that was used for the transportation of the civilian population from Srebrenica. So on the 14th, the day that you wrote this -- or this order was written, what were those trailer trucks doing? How did you know that they were available for transport of this filter the next day on the 15th as we see the order requires?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was precisely what was told to me on the phone. That is the only information that came from that quarter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But surely once you received information from Djukic, you would have looked into getting those trucks, making sure that they were available and making sure that the people that this delivered to, the 27th rear base and the command of the Drina Corps were going to carry it out?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, it wasn't like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you just the got this information, drafted the order, sent it to the 27th and the Drina Corps, and did nothing about making sure it happened? You just forgot about it after that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't forget about that, and this didn't take place as you described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, tell us what you did with this. Were you involved at all in the drafting of this order?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said, it was I who drafted this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was it sent to the 27th rear base and the command of the Drina Corps like it says?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It was sent to the 27th rear base, and to the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you do to determine if this was going to be carried out? We all know that's your job?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't do anything in particular, nor was it necessary for me to do anything. It was sufficient for me to issue an order to the 27th rear base to set up a detail as it's written here to send it to the ground. After that I expected and I received a report on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was that a written report?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was a written report sent by telegraph, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From who?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Lieutenant-Colonel or Colonel, I'm not sure, but his name was Strahinja Jankovic from the 27th rear base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Jankovic reports that he was unable to carry out this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you do about that? Who did you inform?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I could hardly wait to pass on this information to General Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how long after sending this order out did you receive the report from the rear base person? How many days, hours, minutes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot tell you exactly. To the best of my recollection, it might have been after a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you told this to Djukic, was it in person or over the phone?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him that in person. He was at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did he do about it when you told him that this fellow Miroslav Deronjic had blocked his order?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is precisely the reason why I remember this event. He said that he could hardly wait to tell this to General Mladic because that order had been complete foolishness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Djukic was going to tell Mladic that Mladic's order was foolish?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the order. What is foolish about the Drina Corps picking up ammunition and weapons that are left over from an army that is not there anymore? You are in the middle of a war, what is wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the bad thing about this was that General Djukic somehow knew that there was a conflict between the civilian authorities and the army, and that by carrying out this order, this would exacerbate this conflict; and in that sense, he said I told him this was rubbish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what happened? Was this materiel ever inventoried by the army and taken?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, but I'm not sure, but something was done about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What? What was done?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This materiel and equipment left behind was disassembled and stored at the warehouse on the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: By who?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who exactly did that. I don't want to make any assumptions. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Army or civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, the army got possession of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in the end, the army did get this material?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, for example, a big tent which was difficult to disassemble, and there was discussion about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so you were involved in that -- in that process of expropriating this material?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you call it involvement. The information I have is as such as I just told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was this material from the UN base in Srebrenica as it says in the order or the -- more particularly, the UN base in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't personally there. I remember that there were both there but from which particular base and which equipment was taken, I'm not able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Just briefly then, let's go to 65 ter number 3958.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'll give you a hard copy of this, and ... This is a Main Staff order September 26th and your name as the deputy entitled "Expropriation of Material Supplies," and it inventories the stuff from both Srebrenica and Potocari. Is this what you were talking about basically?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, this is what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And just at the end of it, the last page, I just wanted to ask you, we see that it say the initials "RM" and then "/MP." Can you tell us what those mean? And we've heard a lot about what these things mean, I just wanted to check with you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are supposed to be, and they indeed are the initials of the persons who drafted the document, and typed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know why the Main Staff was so involved in this expropriation process as opposed to the Drina Corps by itself?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I wouldn't be able to tell you why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so RM is Ratko Miljanovic and MP is who on these initials?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 5D01113.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is document the Defence showed you that you've talked about a bit already, I think. And this is another one of your documents, as you've stated and dated 19 July. Again this one also has to do with war booty and the transport of people. So is it fair to say you knew about the process to transport the Muslim population out of Zepa on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could have known that the transportation was to be carried out and that is what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Maybe it's a translation issue, but I got that you could have known. Did you or did you not know that the Muslim population was being transported out or planning to be transported out on the 19th of July?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know, or rather, I knew why the buses were commissioned and what the purpose was going to be. But whether the transportation did take place, didn't see any of the sort on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of the negotiations that had taken place and the planning for the Muslim population to start getting on the buses and trucks?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had no knowledge about any plans. As to whether any negotiations were underway, there was some discussion to that effect between General Djukic and the logistics organs at the command post, yes, there were discussions to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you knew there was plans for the Muslims to get on the buses that day?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not what I said, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you didn't know anything about the plans to get the Muslims on the buses that day?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You didn't keep aware of the situation in Zepa? It must have been --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It must have been amazing logistics issues. I mean, we see them; you outline the logistics issues in this very document. Okay. So in paragraph 4, it says: "If need be, Jovanovic shall secure a police unit through the chief of operation and training administration of the Main Staff of the VRS." Now, the chief of the operations and training administration was General Miletic at the time; right.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. Maybe he was there accidently, I don't know. And who actually was there, I cannot tell you. And I didn't understand the question from the first part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was the chief of operations and the training administration of the Main Staff on the 19th of July 1995 when you sent out this order?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was probably General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you mean "probably"? You don't really know?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, who else could it have been?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in that period anyone from the staff could have stood in for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. I was just asking you, who was the person. Who was the chief --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. Who on that particular day was the head of the operations and training administration, don't know whether it was Miletic or someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Surely before you sent out this order involving the chief of operations and training, you would have communicated with that person so that he would be aware that Jovanovic might need to speak with him to get an MP unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. As far as I'm concerned that was not necessary. Colonel Jovanovic was given a clear task. In case of need, and I know what need General Djukic emphasized, he should ask for police security. Police support.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were at the Main Staff, you knew better than I, why would a person in Jovanovic's position go to chief of operations to get a MP support?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, General Djukic issued the clear order to his subordinate Colonel Jovanovic as to what he should do. I'm not going into why it was he who had to do that. I really don't know what to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I take it you are not aware of anyone, yourself or anyone else having any contact with General Miletic about this order?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm certain I had no contact with him concerning this order. I can't speak for others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I take it you had no reason to believe General Miletic did not have the authority to get a military police unit if need be?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at that point in time when General Djukic told me that, that was sufficient for me to draw up this order. I didn't need anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That wasn't my question.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question was, you had no reason to believe that General Miletic did not have the authority to get an MP unit when you wrote this letter, or this order?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the question was put to me in such a way that I really don't understand what you are asking me. I had no reason to believe. As I said, I wasn't interested in that at all, nor was it up to me to take an interest in why General Djukic was issuing an order to me. He had to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, this order went out in your name. The initials for the person that drafted it are yours, the initial of the person that typed it apparently are yours. You are responsible for this order, are you not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as for the drawing up and delivery of this order, yes, I was responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In fact, you heard of the Auto Battalion that was a Main Staff logistics asset; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Auto Battalion was a staff unit, as you said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you told the Defence in getting -- in your meeting with them before coming here that you think the buses that Djukic had told you about were sent to Srebrenica from the Auto Battalion; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I confirm what I said, but they didn't have 50 buses, as far as I can recall, so the question is how many buses were sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let me just read you what the Defence told us and see if you can agree with it. We just want to get this right: "The witness remembers the day when VRS entered into Srebrenica and knows that General Djukic ordered that 50 buses were sent to Potocari. The witness does not know details about that as he was not involved in sending these buses to Srebrenica. However, the witness thinks that these buses are VRS buses which were sent to Srebrenica from Auto Battalion which was a unit directly subordinated to General Djukic. The witness does not have any knowledge about buses that were mobilised from the civilian structures." Do you agree with what the Defence told us about you, what you told them?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what I said, then that's what it was. But I added that I didn't know whether all 50 buses were from the Auto Battalion. There may have been some buses from other units. Those are details. The corps had buses also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, this is serious. Did you or -- do you or do you not agree with what the Defence told us, what I just read to you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say what it says here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you know someone the first name of Rajke, R-a-j-k-e?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rajki or Rajko. Not Rajke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Rajko? Who is Rajko?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rajko could be an organ of the traffic service in the corps. Rajko --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last name, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanovic, could you repeat the last name, please, because the interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, his name was Rajko Krsmanovic, and he was a traffic organ in the corps or desk officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We've got an intercept that I want to ask you about. Does the town Milosevici mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, your order that we just talked about on the 19th of July was received by somebody at 1.50 a.m. on the 20th, so it looks like that order went out fairly late on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So let's now go, having that in mind, go to 65 ter 1271D is the English and it's 1271C in the B/C/S. Let me give you a typed version of that so you don't have to try to follow the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This was intercepted that same day at 2116 hours, so late in the day on the 19th, not really fairly close to your order likely. And if you could take sometime to look at it.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, do I have to read it all?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please. It's not very long. You'll see, it's a simple intercept. I don't think there's anything very controversial in it, as you read. We've heard about the buses in your previous order and Borike and Sjeversko and the organising of those buses, or 50 vehicles. We see mention of the 63rd, that's the Auto Battalion out of Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume, yes, the 63rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we know what the 27th logistics base is.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a couple of people, Rajke is what the Muslims heard, and Goran, and Kerkez. You've already told us about Kerkez that was in logistics. And they clearly are talking about the organisation of these vehicles, and on the second page of the English, you can see that they start about: "Let it be around 9.30 in the sector of Sjeversko," which we've learned from other witnesses is right here Borike. And then it goes on and next says, "To Sjeversko, then they will split them in Borike to the left and right. Borike --"

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't follow what is being read out. I haven't found where it is, what you reading out now. Can you help me find it please, where is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, it's not -- look for the word Koscanica in parentheses, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sjeversko or Koscanica, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the bottom of the first page in your draft, the first bottom of the first page.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. If that's on page 2, on page 2 in my version, 2, 4, 6, 8, it's the 16th line from the top. Koscanica in parenthesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why don't you hand it back to me sir, and I'll show you. Or you can read it on the screen, it's right near the bottom. Third line up from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, but in the version I have, it's on page 2 line 16, the typed text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well just follow it along. If it's easier to go on the computer. And you'll see it says, "To Sjeversko, then they will split them in Borike to the left and right, do you understand." Then we need to go to page 2 in the B/C/S it says in Borike, X says, "Yes." Kerkez says, "All right." X says, "Well, that would be all." Kerkez says, "Carry out your part like you did last time." X says, "I'm dealing with it." Kerkez says, "Although I think it will probably be less." X says, "All right. They are looking again for 50 to 70 vehicles, do you understand?" Kerkez says, "All right, all right." And X says, "So that the transport could be carried out in one round." Are you following this?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honours, now I'm following.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then Kerkez says, "In one round." X says, "Yes, most likely." Kerkez, "All right." X, "Yes." Kerkez, "Deadline is at 14 hours but we'll tell them it is at 12." X says, "But where?" Kerkez says, "Yes." X says, "What? At 12 ... At 10 all vehicles should be in Sjeversko." Kerkez says, "Miljanovic just told me." X says, "Listen." Kerkez says, "Yes." X says, "I've just received the order from General Krstic." Kerkez says, "Yes." X says, "That's what he is asking for." And Kerkez says, "That is probably some reserve. Here, Miljanovic told me that the agreement was to start loading at 14 hours." And then it goes and talks about starting to start loading and arranging it from Rogatica, and I'll stop there for now. It's the Prosecution's position that this is happening at the same time your last order, and that this is people organising the vehicles to take the Muslim population out of Zepa and they want to do it in one round, and that we know you were knowledge somewhat of this just from your previous order. So does this help you refresh your recollection that you were aware that there had been agreement that the Muslims would start loading at a certain time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't know about any agreement, nor did I know the point in time when the Muslims would board or whether they would board.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And as we go over to the next page, there's some talk and the Muslims hear it as "Balasevic," must know that, it's fine. And X says, "Is Bosic over there?" And Kerkez says, "He is on duty on 175. All right 175." There is -- we have evidence in this case which is 65 ter 3011, which I don't need to bring up, that on the 19th of July, Tomislav Basevic, the logistics man from the Drina Corps is the duty officer, and that 175 in another exhibit is the secure line at the Drina Corps. So let me ask you, did you have any contact with Mr. Basevic regarding these vehicles for the transport of Muslims from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't remember any contact with Basa, that is Mr. Basevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another document, 65 ter number 41. And I'll ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this is a document, there's a translation error, it shouldn't be General Staff of the army. It should be Main Staff of the army up at the top. It's dated 14 July [sic], and it's noted to be urgent. And it's under the name of General Mladic; and it's to the attention of the command of the Drina Corps, and to the logistics sector of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. And a copy to the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade for their information, and it says: "This is to approve 5 tons of D-2 diesel fuel for carrying out engineering works in the zone of the responsibility of the Drina Corps. The logistics sector of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska shall deliver the fuel to the standard barracks in Zvornik, to Captain Milorad Trpic. Captain Trpic shall be responsible for the accurate maintenance of records on the number of engine work hours of engineering machines and account accordingly for consumption of fuel." Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry I would just like to make a correction on page 16 line 9 it's a 14th of September. Not the 14th of July. I would just like to make that correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose you agree to that, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolute correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, clearly this is addressed to your sector. It says that your sector, the Main Staff logistics sector shall deliver this fuel directly to the barracks in Zvornik. Now, surely General Mladic would have spoken to someone to get the details of this before signing off on an order with such detail. Do you have knowledge of this, anything about this?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no knowledge whatsoever about this order, absolutely none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there anything unusual about this order? For example, is it normal for the -- for Mladic to order fuel directly to a brigade to a security officer?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't understand the question. I don't know where Mladic was issuing the order from. I'm not going into where Mladic was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question had nothing to do with where Mladic was. You may recall spending a fair amount of time in direct examination talking about brigades not going directly to the Main Staff; so I'm just asking you, is it unusual for the Main Staff to send something directly to the brigade? If that's what is happening, maybe it's not, and if you don't know, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I understood the order well, when General Mladic issues orders, then nothing is unusual. He also issued orders to individuals directly wherever he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Looking at the top of this order, it's number 03-4. Do you know what Main Staff branch that is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I wouldn't be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we know, and we know that that is the administration for operations and training that in September 14th General Miletic was the head of. So this particular order, I take it, would not have been drafted by the logistics sector, it would have been drafted by the operations and training sector that General Miletic was involved in heading?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, what is the question that you are asking me? You are just stating an assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want you to either disagree or agree. We've been doing that a long time, you should be getting used to it.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot agree with you. Perhaps you know something about that, but I don't, and that's a huge difference. I have to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you think it's possible the logistics sector may have drafted this and not the operations and training sector of Miletic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, not in the wildest dreams could this have been written in the logistics sector and then sent by Mladic. I don't know who signed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why not in the wildest dreams could the logistics sector be involved in something like this? Sending fuel sounds radical, what is the problem with that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in response to your questions yesterday and the day before yesterday, I said that I never put my signature under the name of General Djukic. And I don't know who in the logistics would put their signature under the name of Ratko Mladic. It is totally incomprehensible to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not talking about putting anybody's signature anywhere. Just asking you why is it so wild to think that the logistics unit was involved in sending this fuel to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is not what I said. I'm repeating again. No one can send such a telegram from the logistics and put Ratko Mladic's name on it. Whether someone took part in drafting this situation with the fuel, I said nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are not quite sure what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They are not alone in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we want to make sure. I think I leave it in your hands, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you any more about who drafted it; we know who drafted it. I'm not asking you about who sent it out; we know who sent it out. I'm asking you if the logistics unit was involved in sending the fuel pursuant to this order?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question. I don't know whether the logistics sector of the Main Staff was involved in the execution of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could they have been?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you in your position should have known about it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I, in my position in the logistics sector of the Main Staff of the VRS, was not obliged to have any knowledge about this transaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter number 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's another Main Staff document. Same date, 14 September 1995. From the logistics centre this time, the technical division with a number that we are familiar with, 10. And we see in this order it mentions: "Pursuant to the order of the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska immediately issue the following quantity of fuel to the Drina Corps Command, 5.000 litres." I take it 5 tons equals 5.000 litres?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Is 5 tons the same as 5.000 litres?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many litres in a ton?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you that 5.000 litres equals 5 tons. I just wanted to make sure whether that was your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And is this logistics document under the name of Colonel Zarko Zjubojevic related in your mind to the previous Mladic order?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is what this document says, and there's a number 03/4-241; and he is making reference to the previous one that you showed me earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And correct me if I'm wrong, but I'm sure you know nothing whatsoever about this that went out of the logistics sector, am I right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about this. This is the first time that I've seen this and that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, it's the -- I put my case to you, is that I don't believe you are telling the truth, but on that note I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He should answer that, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in fact that's why I switched on my microphone. Do you wish to comment on what Mr. McCloskey has just told you? Do you wish to answer? He is alleging that you are --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey has just told you, in your face, that he is not believing you. In other words, that you haven't been saying the truth, speaking the truth. What is your answer to that, if you wish to give us an answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I would like to take this opportunity and say that this document that's been shown to me and the actions described in them is something that I have heard about and seen for the first time today, and that is my truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Ms. Fauveau, is there redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we could keep in document on the screen for the time being. In this document we see that it stems from the technical department. Was the technical department under your authority?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, it was not under my authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you have any reason to know everything, or rather, did you know what the technical department was doing?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had no reason to interfere with the operation of the technical department or to have knowledge about what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When General Djukic was present in 1995 in Han Pijesak when he was holding a position there. Were you made aware of what General Djukic was doing?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had knowledge about his activities only to the extent that he was prepared to give this information to me. I'm not a person of inquisitive nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... D361 to the witness, please. 5D361 is the document I'd like to show to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is a directive which you have talked about twice already.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need page 7, please, in B/C/S, and 8 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Item 6.6, yesterday when I put the question to you who could have written this paragraph, and you answered by saying General Djukic. Could General Djukic have written this paragraph without mentioning it to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. What is the problem, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours. At the time when this document was drafted, this witness stood in for General Djukic, and from his answer we can see that he started standing in for him since 29 March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... is dated the 31st of March. It doesn't mean that it was written on the 31st of March --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was a lot of noise in the courtroom, the interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, I couldn't follow you either, Ms. Fauveau. So I would kindly ask you to repeat then I'll give the floor to Mr. McCloskey, and then we'll decide what to do. If you could repeat your response to the objection raised by Mr. Krgovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is a dated the 31st of March, which does not mean that it was not drafted a few days prior to that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I never brought that document up. I don't believe my counsels did. This general idea --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- about this witness doesn't know everything that Djukic knows is fine. I'll stipulate to that, but the going back into documents we bring up issues exactly like the one Mr. Krgovic has brought out. Are we going to need out when it was drafted and all that? I didn't bring it up, why are we getting into this? The probative value of this witness on these topics I think is minimal and not worth wasting time on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my colleague from the Gvero team has suggested that this document was not written by the logistics sector or in the logistics sector, so I'm entitled to put the question to him as part of my redirect, and this was yesterday on page 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But my question is, you are asking him could General Djukic have written this paragraph without mentioning it to you? Isn't it speculative in itself? What can he answer you?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. My colleague put the question to him, and General Djukic did not tell you or issue instructions for to you prepare any proposals in connection with that. My question ties into the question which was put by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanovic, if you could answer the question without speculating, then please go ahead. But if you don't know, just tell us so, and we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would appreciate the question to be repeated to me in order for me to have it clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could General Djukic have written paragraph 6.6 without mentioning it to you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, he could have done that, or could do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday my colleague read out General Djukic statement to you. In this statement General Djukic said that he, himself, General Gvero set up Salapura, Maric disagreed with Mladic. You told us before that General Djukic was stationed in Han Pijesak. Where was Salapura based? Do you know who he is first of all?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Salapura was an intelligence officer with the Main Staff of the VRS, as far as I know. Maybe somebody else has different information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Where was his department based?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This administration was based in Crna Rijeka at the main command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As far as Maric is concerned, where was he? M-A-R-I-C.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am just waiting for the transcript. Maric was also stationed in Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What about Gvero?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same applies to General Gvero, he was in Crna Rijeka. General Mladic was in Crna Rijeka as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It was suggested to you that there was no meeting between the commander and his associates. So General Djukic who was based in Han Pijesak, how could you know that this person in Crna Rijeka disagreed with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly not overlap for interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you answer this question without speculating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how he knows about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You also said yesterday that General Djukic's statement was in line with what you told the investigators of the OTP. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I agreed with a part of General Djukic's statement read out to me. I don't have a chance to see the statement in its entirety. If you are referring to the part that you have just mentioned now, then all I can say is that General Djukic often protested against the orders issues by General Mladic in my presence, and he often expressed dissatisfaction with certain moves and actions; but I didn't want to get involved into that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: All right. My question was not question precise. How did you know about those people in Crna Rijeka: Salapura Maric and General Gvero. How did you know that these people disagreed with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agreed with the opinion of General Djukic. I didn't want to go into what kind of relationships are there between other generals and this Colonel Salapura that has just been mentioned. Whether my opinion coincide with the opinion about Maric as a personality, but not for a moment did I presume to know what were the relationships between General Mladic and General Gvero and General Mladic and Miletic and Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You were asked several questions about Zepa. Do you know whether General Djukic went to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if General Djukic was in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show the witness Exhibit number 1402. I apologise for the fact that this document has not been translated, and this is an intercept dated 26 of July 1995. 5D1402. That is the exhibit number. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We can see at the beginning of this intercept, first of all, the date which is the 26th of July 1995; and then we can see this is a conversation that took place at 13 hours 10. General Djukic talks to Vukic [as interpreted] Rajko and Ratko and in brackets it says, "The general is probably Mladic." For the sake of the record since we don't have a translation I shall read the relevant part of this intercept. If we could show the bottom part. It's in the middle of the page, can you see this after the letter D where it says "Djukic"?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just give me a minute, please. Djukic, yeah, and before that Ratko or Rajko, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it's right there. And then the conversation continues: "Rajko, tell me please is my boss there?" Answer: "Yes, but he is resting. You will have to wait for awhile. If you can wait, I'd like to ask you something you need not talk to him." "Yes." "You were present when he ordered you for these men of mine, a group, to go there, he said, but I don't know, he didn't say where they should report to him." "Yes, I was present. He is coming, the general heard you. He will be here shortly." Then we have the conversation between General Djukic and General Mladic. General Mladic said, "Djuka, hello. General Djukic, "Greetings, boss." Then it's Mladic, "How are you?" Djukic's answer, "Very well, thank you." Then Mladic, "Is your health good?"

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move on to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Djukic said, "All is fine, but these men told me that my group should arrive there only they are not certain to what sector." And then Mladic said, "Let them come to Boksanica at UNPROFOR checkpoint number 2." And Djukic said, "Okay." Mladic added, "By Rogatica." Then Djukic, "Very well." And then Mladic told him, "You can take a walk as well." Then Djukic said, "I'd love to, but I don't know." And then he said, "I'm coming." And a bit later, "By the way, I need something to agree with you." And then Mladic told him, "Agreed and bring with you the papers that need to be signed." And Mladic added, "And see with Krbic and Miletic what papers need to be signed."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so too. So let's have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I start, the Prosecutor informed me during the break that the document I used just now, 5D1401 [sic], is document P1358C in the e-court system and that there is an English translation of this document. I'm sorry I wasted the Chambers time with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, you stated that you did not know that General Djukic went to the Zepa region. Did you know that on the 26th of July, General Mladic was this at that region, was in the Zepa region?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know where General Mladic was in August and September 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember, Your Honours. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What was the most critical frontline at the time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was the area around Sarajevo and the most critical situation was in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know whether General Mladic went to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that General Mladic had been to the Krajina on many occasions, but I cannot confirm that he was there on this particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember where General Djukic was in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I cannot remember that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you go to the Krajina in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about August 1995, I was in Banja Luka. Whether I went any further than that, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you went in Banja Luka or somewhere else, were you able to send the documents you were supposed to send? As a general rule, were you in a position to send documents when you were away from the logistics command post from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question. Wherever I was, I was able to send any document I wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What did you put in the heading of the document?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I had this need, I put in the heading Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, sector for the rear. The initial numbers, whatever they were, I can't recall now, the date, the contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: All right. That's enough. When did you see General Djukic for the last time before he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was sometime between the 1st and the 15th of January 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And at the time, what was his health condition like?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, General Djukic was ill, but he didn't appear to be ill.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, madam. Judge Kwon? Judge Stole? Mr. Miljanovic, we have come to the end of your testimony. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I thank you for coming over to give evidence, and I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Documents? There are nine documents which the Miletic Defence team wishes to tender. The list has been circulated. Mr. McCloskey, do you have any objections to any of these documents? Yes, madam, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Instead of document 5D1401, I seek the admission of document P1358C. It's already been translated and it's exactly the same document as 5D1401.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That makes things easier. Thank you, madam. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clear up the numbers, that was originally 5D1402, not 01, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise, you don't have any objections to any of these nine documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So they are all admitted. There are no documents from the other Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We have got one, Your Honour. The list has been circulated, it's 6D234.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It hasn't reached us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It was the laws that were put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see okay. Do you have any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is also admitted. Then we have the Prosecution list, which has also been circulated. Any objections, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Other Defence teams, any objections? So all these documents are also all admitted. And we can proceed with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that this witness should be notified of his rights pursuant to rule 90 (b) of the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 90 (e) not (b). For the record, now, I notice the presence of Mr. Thayer amongst the Prosecution team and of Mr. Haynes for General Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Pandurevic, any time you need to leave the courtroom, you only please need to tell us. Good morning, to you, Mr. Masal, and welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Defence team for General Miletic has summoned you as a Defence witness. Before you start giving evidence, you are required to make a solemn declaration according to our rules to the effect that you will be testifying this oath. The text is being handed to you now, please read it out allowed, and that will be your solemn commitment with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are here as a witness to answer all the questions that will be put to you both by the Defence team for General Miletic, and others, including the Prosecution. I don't know what questions you will be asked. But there is a possibility that you may be asked questions which if you answer truthfully, as per the solemn declaration that you have just made, if you answer truthfully, that could possibly lead to some kind of investigation and also criminal proceedings against you. I'm not saying that this will happen. I'm not saying that there will be such questions. But I cannot exclude such questions being possibly made to you either. If such questions are made to you and in your mind you feel that if you answer them you would be incriminating yourself or exposing yourself to criminal proceedings, then you have a right under our rules to ask us, the Judges in this case, to exempt you from answering such questions. You need to be specific, you need to tell us that you wish not to answer such questions because you consider them incriminatory. We will then decide whether to grant you such exemption or not because your right is not absolute. If we decide to exempt you from answering such questions, that's fine. But we could also decide to order you to answer such questions. In such a case you have a further right, and that is that whatever you may have stated in reply to questions which we order you to answer, cannot be then made use of against you in any criminal proceedings that may be taken against you. Is that clear? Is that a clear explanation of your right, or do you want me to expand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you are right clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we can start. Ms. Fauveau will be asking you some questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, could you please state your first name and last name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Dragisa Masal.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please tell us briefly about your educational background, what schools you went to and so on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: I completed a civilian secondary school, and then the military academy, the command staff academy, and the school of national defence, the last three were all military schools.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What positions did you hold before the beginning of the war in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Before the beginning of the war in the former Yugoslavia, I held the post of commander of an artillery platoon, battery commander, commander of artillery battalion, of a regiment, then chief of artillery in a mechanised brigade, and chief of artillery in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When did you join the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: I joined the Army of Republika Srpska as soon as it was formed. That is from the 12th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What positions did you hold in the Army of Republika Srpska between the 12th of May 1992 and the end of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: In the Army of Republika Srpska, I was the commander of an artillery regiment, the commander of the Visegrad tactical group and the chief of artillery in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us what rank you had when you joined the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: I was colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When were you promoted to the rank of general?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: I was promoted to the rank of general after the war. To major-general in 1998 and to lieutenant-general in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just briefly, can you tell us what positions you held after the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: After the war, I was appointed chief of the sector for organisation, mobilisation, and personnel affairs in the General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to your position of commander of the tactical group of Visegrad. When did you become commander of the Visegrad tactical group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: I became commander of the Visegrad tactical group on the 4th of February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And until when did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: I held that position until the 20th of August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What was the area of responsibility of the Visegrad tactical group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: My area of responsibility or rather the area of responsibility of the Visegrad tactical group corresponded to the territory of five municipalities in the upper Podrinje area and these were the municipalities of Rogatica, Visegrad, Rudo, Cajnice, and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were a commander of the Visegrad tactical group, who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: My immediate superior was the commander of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You stated that in 1993 you were the commander of the Visegrad tactical group, were you aware of agreements related to protected areas in Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: With respect to the agreements related to protected areas, I was not directly familiar with those, but through orders coming from the superior command as the commander of the tactical group, I was fully informed of the establishment of the protected areas of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you receive specific instructions from your higher command related to these protected areas?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: I received an order on the signing of a ceasefire between the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, that is General Mladic, and of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina General Halilovic, and the commander of UNPROFOR. With respect to the cessation of hostilities and the declaration or rather the establishment of protected areas, the protected areas of Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, Tuzla, and Bihac, these were part of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show the witness Exhibit 5D1200. It's an order coming from the Main Staff dated 8th of May 1993, on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde, and on the cessation of any type of military activity in these areas. Could we have page 2 in English. I'm interested in point 4 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, under this point mention is made of the creation of commissions to monitor the demilitarisation. Were you aware of the existence of these commissions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Yes, I received this order as the commander of the tactical group in view of the fact that I was duty-bound to designate people from my command, from my unit, to the commissions in the areas of Zepa and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please turn to page 2 in B/C/S, and page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At point 4 .3 related to Gorazde, we can see indeed that an officer from the Visegrad tactical group is to be appointed; and when it comes to point 4.2 related to Zepa, do you recognise the names of the people who are mentioned as being part of this commission?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Yes. I designated from my unit Luka Dragicevic, who was a lieutenant-colonel and an interpreter for the English language. I would also like to add that I designated from my unit for the commission for the Zepa area Major Radomir Furtula, who was a member of the commission. He was then the Chief of Staff of the Rogatica Brigade and also an interpreter for the English language.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification, you mentioned Luka Dragicevic and the interpreter for the English language when you are talking about the two persons, you are talking about the Gorazde commission. Did the Zepa commission actually work, was it effective?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President I wanted to note for my friend, I think the witness answered her question and it was reflected for a second but then disappeared from the transcript as to whether he was referring to both the interpreter for the English language and another individual. I thought I heard him say yes, and I think it was actually in the transcript for a minute. It's not there, I don't know if that's the case or not, but I just wanted to bring that up before we move too further along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's would probably be best if I repeated the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, for the record, you talked about Luka Dragicevic and an interpreter for the English language. Were these two individuals member of the Gorazde commission?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to talk about the Zepa commission. Did this commission actually work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: This commission was established and on several occasions, it spent time in Zepa with a view to carrying out the tasks it had been assigned with respect to the demilitarisation of the Zepa protected area. However, after some 15 days or so of work, that commission ceased to function because the overall activities in the protected area of Zepa as regards demilitarisation or the withdrawal of weapons by the Muslim forces had no results.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What was the situation in relation to the Gorazde commission?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: The commission for Gorazde was established, but it never actually went to Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you item 7 which you have in front of you in B/C/S. In English this will be on page 4. This is page 3, it's item 7 I'm interested in. At the top of page 4. I am sorry, this should be at the bottom of page 3. We can read: [In English] "Members of the so-called army of BiH once weapons or handed over, are to be treated like any other civilians with freedom of movement provided for all so that they can if they wish leave the said regions or remain there." [Interpretation] At the time you received this order, was the army of the Republika Srpska ready to fulfill what is mentioned at item 7?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: We sincerely believed in this agreement on the cessation of hostilities, and we felt that it was a good beginning to putting an end to the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The orders of the superior command were orders we took seriously, and we complied with them and carried out all the tasks in order to preserve the ceasefire and make it possible to achieve the final goal which was the end of the war through peaceful political means. And we complied with the orders consistently.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you Exhibit number 5D1027, which is another order stemming from the staff of the Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska dated the 9th of May 1993, and which relates also to the agreement signed on the 8th of May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At item 1 week see that the ceasefire on the entire territory of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina should come into effect at noon on the 9th of May 1993, but what I'm interested in is item 2 and more specific here, the first two sentences. We can see that it is said one should not fire back if the enemy opens fire, and one should only respond if the infantry or tanks attack in an organised manner. Can you tell us when you needed to fire back and when you shouldn't fire back? As far as I'm concerned, I'm not a military person and this is not very clear to me.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: The order issued by the Main Staff is precise. Based on this order, all the commands were obliged to inform all members up to the last soldier with the content of this order. This item stipulates in detail that refraining from responding to enemy artillery fire, and lesser provocations should be done because the combat readiness on the positions of units is such that if artillery fire, if it is a provocation only, the units can be protected and find cover. Then it goes on to say that only in the event of an organised infantry or tank attacks, meaning that all the units must accept combat if it is a serious attack, in order to secure the existing positions. This is the essence of this item in this order. As far as this is concerned, all my commands and units strictly followed this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you Exhibit number 5D1025. This is an order stemming from the staff of the Main Staff dated the 11th of May 1993. We are still talking about the agreements and the demilitarised zones.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you read item 3, please, which starts with: "Demilitarised zone will be controlled by UNPROFOR."

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At the time, i.e., in May 1993, you at least since you were the commander of the Visegrad tactical group and part of the Army Republika Srpska, did you think that the -- that UNPROFOR would fulfill its tasks? Let me repeat my question. In 1993, the army of the Republika Srpska and you as a commander of the Visegrad tactical group, did you believe that UNPROFOR would fulfill its tasks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Initially we believed that the agreement would be implemented as a whole, that is to say, that implementation of the agreement would begin. However, after the first visit by the commission to Zepa and particularly due to the fact that the Gorazde commission never went on the ground, or, rather, it was never invited to go to Gorazde, we realised that the Muslim forces and the Muslim command and UNPROFOR as well, this agreement was actually a farce in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd now like to show you the last order. Exhibit number 5D1026 is the last order in this batch. I would like to show you two exhibits, but it's one in the same order. This is order dated 14th of May 1993. 02/2-420.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you look at the bottom of this document, of this order. Who was this order sent out to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you receive this order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, the copy we have in B/C/S is not very legible. Could we show the witness Exhibit number 1202, which is the same order, and which is a signed version of this same order.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General, can you confirm that this order is an identical order to the one you've seen previously, save for the fact that this one is a signed order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Yes, that's an identical order. This is an original bearing the signature of the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I'm particularly interested in is item 1 of this order, which reads: [In English] "Enable unhindered passage of and protection of consignments, equipment and personnel providing aid intended for the civilian population of the opposing side." [Interpretation] You said that you were in the area of Zepa and Gorazde. Did your units abide by this order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: My units in our area of responsibility follow the orders to the full, i.e., we strictly abided by the Main Staff's order on the cessation of combat operations and on the respect of the borders of the protected areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, as far as passage of aid is concerned, that was intended for the civilian population of the opposite side. What was the situation like?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: There were no problems for the convoys of humanitarian organisations to pass through as well as the evacuation convoys or those delivering any staff to Zepa and other zones. Their routes were precisely determined and there were also checkpoints where they were inspected. And we knew exactly along which routes and at what times they would pass.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We shall get back to the issue of the convoys a little bit later. Could you now look at paragraph 2, please, where we discuss misappropriation of some of the aid for military teary purposes. Why was this order drafted like this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: The reason for including this kind of stipulation into this order was probably reports from the ground and intelligence confirming that in certain combat zones and areas, the infrastructure required for the normal day-to-day life of civilians was being abused; and it was actually used as an instrument to exert pressure on the civilian population. Specifically in my area, we did not have under our control any installations that could have impact on the protected area such as the sources of drinking water, et cetera, or facilities for the production of certain fuels. The only problem that existed was the electric grid which in the whole area was largely damaged and could not have been fixed and restored in a very short time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We have seen the orders given by the army of the Republika Srpska relating to the agreements on -- pertaining to the demilitarised zones. Could you tell us what the attitude of the army of the ABiH was vis-a-vis these agreements?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: We sincerely anticipated and expected that the command of the BH Army would take a serious approach to the implementation of this agreement. However, and precisely because the commission was not accepted and was denied entry to Gorazde, we finally realised that their intention was not to stop the war; but rather their own intention was to bide time and place certain areas step by step under the protection of the UN forces, and to regroup the forces from these areas and dispatch them to other regions to carry out combat operations. We practically could feel that coming from the so-called protected area of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you a few orders that are dated 1993. I shall not go into these in detail. The first one is 5D1264.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is an order which stems from the tactical group in Visegrad and which is dated 12th of November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 2 in English, please. Could we show the witness the bottom of page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is an order which bears your name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he can read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let's look at item 3, please, which addresses TGD. This is a sabotage group and terrorism group in Zepa. I'm not interested in the details of all of it, but you remember anything about this order and a situation in which armed groups were leaving Zepa?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Just a minor correction, this should read subversive and terrorist group. That's what TGD stands for. The reason was on several occasions from the direction of the protected area of Zepa and from Gorazde, these sabotage terrorist groups were infiltrated into my area of responsibility; and their task was to render the roads impassable to hinder or make uncertain and unsafe any movement within the depth of the territory, and to keep our units under constant tension. This order was precisely proceeded by such a terrorist and sabotage action on the Kopito pass on the Rogatica road. They planted an anti-tank mine in the pot hole on the road. The mine was hit by a vehicle and the three members of the VRS who were in the car were seriously injured. In addition to these events, we received intelligence and gathered information that such groups are continually being prepared both in Zepa and Srebrenica.
